      <content name="title">Developmental Disabilities</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Mental Retardation</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What are developmental disabilities?<p>Developmental disabilities are conditions that are usually present at birth. They can affect a child's growth and development. These conditions can cause physical, learning, language, or behavior issues. They can include:</p><ul><li>Learning disabilities. These conditions affect the ability to learn.</li><li>Autism spectrum disorder (ASD). This is a disorder that affects behavior, communication, and social skills.</li><li>Cerebral palsy (CP). This is a condition that affects movement, coordination, and balance.</li><li>Physical disabilities. These could include blindness or deafness.</li><li>Conditions that can affect both physical and mental abilities. This could include Down <span class="qt1">syndrome</span>.</li></ul><p>These conditions can cause lifelong challenges in learning. Completing daily tasks may be difficult. Early treatment may help your child learn important skills and make the most of their strengths.</p>What causes developmental disabilities?<p>Developmental disabilities are often present at birth. They can occur due to various reasons. These can include:</p><ul><li>Genetic or chromosome abnormalities. These cause conditions such as Down <span class="qt1">syndrome</span>, Fragile-X-<span class="qt1">Syndrome</span>, and Rett <span class="qt1">syndrome</span>.</li><li>Use of substances while pregnant. For example, drinking alcohol when pregnant can cause fetal alcohol spectrum disorders.</li><li>Certain infections during pregnancy.</li><li>Preterm birth or low birth weight.</li></ul>How are developmental disabilities diagnosed?<p>The way a developmental disability is diagnosed depends on the condition. Screening tests or a physical exam may be done to check for a medical problem. Other tests and questionnaires may help find out if your child has a developmental disability. These may include:</p><ul><li>Screening tests that are done during pregnancy or for newborns</li><li>Developmental and behavioral screening tests or questionnaires  to check if your child is developing on schedule</li><li>Observing your child's behavior and how they interact with other people</li><li>Testing your child's intellectual and school performance</li><li>Asking about your family history</li></ul>What are the treatments for developmental disabilities?<p>If your child has a developmental disability, these are usually lifelong conditions. Often, there is no cure, but treatment can help the symptoms. Treatments can include:</p><ul><li>Physical, speech, and occupational therapy</li><li>Special teaching methods</li><li>Psychological counseling</li><li>To keep track of how your child grows and changes over time</li></ul><p>NIH: National Institute of Child Health and Human Development</p></content>

    <document rank="1" url="https://medlineplus.gov/movementdisorders.html">
      <content name="title">Movement Disorders</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Ataxia</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Chorea</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Dyskinesia</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Tardive Dyskinesia</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Movement disorders are neurologic conditions that cause problems with movement, such as:</p><ul><li>Increased movement that can be voluntary (intentional) or involuntary (unintended)</li><li>Decreased or slow voluntary movement</li></ul><p>There are many different movement disorders. Some of the more common types include:</p><ul><li>Ataxia, the loss of muscle coordination</li><li>Dystonia, in which involuntary contractions of your muscles cause twisting and repetitive movements. The movements can be painful.</li><li>Huntington's disease, an inherited disease that causes nerve cells in certain parts of the brain to waste away. This includes the nerve cells that help to control voluntary movement.</li><li>Parkinson's disease, which is a disorder that slowly gets worse over time. It causes tremors, slowness of movement, and trouble walking.</li><li>Tourette <span class="qt1">syndrome</span>, a condition that causes people to make sudden twitches, movements, or sounds (tics)</li><li>Tremor and essential tremor, which cause involuntary trembling or shaking movements. The movements may be in one or more parts of your body.</li></ul><p>Causes of movement disorders include:</p><ul><li>Genetics</li><li>Infections</li><li>Medicines</li><li>Damage to the brain, spinal cord, or peripheral nerves</li><li>Metabolic disorders</li><li>Stroke and vascular diseases</li><li>Toxins</li></ul><p>Treatment varies by disorder. Medicines can cure some disorders. Others get better when an underlying disease is treated. Often, however, there is no cure. In that case, the goal of treatment is to improve symptoms and relieve pain.</p></content>
